newsitem.title: CANADA: Royal Oak says dispute endangers Kemess.
newsitem.headline: Royal Oak says dispute endangers Kemess.

text.p: Royal Oak Mines Inc said Friday that a dispute with the British Columbia government is jeopardizing its Kemess copper-gold mine project.
Royal Oak president Peggy Witte told a news conference that the company has several options if the dispute is not resolved.

These include cancelling the C$390 million project -- which she said would not be in the best interests of shareholders -- going to court or seeking alternative financing to raise C$151.5 million that would have come from the government.

Witte said the province had appointed Charles Kang, a deputy minister, to negotiate with the company on the dispute and gave Royal Oak indications that "something should be resolved in the next two to four weeks."

The dispute centers on a 1995 agreement the mining company struck with the province. That deal compensated the company for the cancellation of the Windy Craggy copper project and paved the way for development of Kemess in northern British Columbia. Royal Oak said the province had pledged C$166 million in economic assistance and direct compensation to Kemess.
The government and company are at odds over interpretation of that 1995 pact and about C$25 million of the government's C$166 million contribution are at issue in the dispute.
The government has so far paid the company C$14.5 million but is delaying further payment because of the disagreement. Royal Oak said C$7.8 million is currently due.

Royal Oak said it did not resume work at the Kemess site on January 7 as scheduled after a Christmas break because of the dispute. But Witte announced Friday that Royal Oak would resume construction in the hopes of a resolution to the dispute.

She was reluctant to be specific about the exact nature of the dispute but said there were three primary areas of difference in interpretation over the 1995 accord. These include stumpage payments to the government for cutting of trees to build a power line to the site and calculation of royalty payments to the government. "We have tried for 10 months to negotiate these items," she said.

Witte castigated the government, saying it had not lived up to its agreement, and speculated the province has dragged its feet so the company would ultimately feel forced to give in because of its growing financial commitment to the mine.
But she vowed Royal Oak would not "cave or compromise. Certainly this company is not going to do that...We have other remedies."
She said the company would seek to hold the government liable for any damages such as the costs of shareholder dilution or increased borrowing if the company sought more financing for Kemess.
Royal Oak has so far spent C$140 million of the mine's C$390 million projected capital cost. She said Kemess was currently on budget and on track for an April 1998 start up.
Kemess is about 40 percent complete, Witte said.
But without a resolution of its dispute Royal Oak would put its money to work on two projects already underway in Ontario, she said. Exploration in British Columbia has been suspended, she said.
Yet Witte said she was hopeful that Kang's appointment would speed a resolution of the dispute.

Kemess, considered a core asset key to Royal Oak's growth plans, is estimated to contain mineable reserves of 4.1 million ounces of gold and one billion pounds of copper. The mine would have an estimated 20-year life.

In response to Witte's attack, British Columbia Minister of Investment Dan Miller said it was "highly inappropriate to try to think that negotiating through the media has any impact whatsoever." He told local radio that the government would let the negotiations take their course.
Witte said the maximum amount that appeared to be under dispute with the government was C$25 million.
Separately, she said "substantially all" Royal Oak's 1997 gold production was hedged at US$395 an ounce.
